title: Caieta (Gaeta), Aeneas' nurse
greek: Tu quoque litoribus nostris, Aeneia nutrix, / aeternam moriens famam, Caieta, dedisti
short: Aeneas' old nurse dies and gives her name to the harbour of Caieta, modern Gaeta, on the border of Latium and Campania.
body: Book VII opens with a death and a place-name, a pattern already set by Misenus (6.234-235) and Palinurus (6.381-383): each loss is repaid with a name that lasts on the Italian map. 'Thou also' (tu quoque) links Caieta to those two. The poem keeps explaining Italian names by Trojan stories (an aetiology), so that the landscape itself seems to remember Aeneas. Conington notes that the place lay near Formiae and that a nurse held real standing in old families; the nurse also recalls Homer's Eurycleia, Odysseus' nurse. Ovid gives her epitaph (Met. 14.441-444). The narrator's aside 'if that be glory' (si qua est ea gloria) is a muted note: the comfort of a name over the dead is real but small. Ancient writers also knew a rival derivation of the name, so Virgil is choosing the Trojan version.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 7.1
Ovid, Metamorphoses 14.441-444 (Caieta's epitaph)
Virgil, Aeneid 7.1, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)

title: Circe's land (Circeii)
greek: Proxima Circaeae raduntur litora terrae, / dives inaccessos ubi Solis filia lucos ...
short: The Trojans sail past Monte Circeo, the promontory the Romans identified with the island of Homer's Circe, daughter of the Sun.
body: Circe is the witch of Odyssey 10, who turns Odysseus' men into swine; in Homer her house is surrounded by tame wolves and lions (Od. 10.210-219). The Romans located her at Circeii, a high headland south of Antium. Virgil makes the beasts cry out in chains, men 'disfashioned' into animals, and has Neptune carry the Trojans past: this is the last Odyssean danger before the Iliadic half begins. Circe matters for Book VII: Hesiod already makes Latinus a son of Circe and Odysseus (Theogony 1011-1013), and later in this book Circe turns King Picus into a woodpecker (7.189-191) and the fire-breathing horses that Latinus sends to Aeneas are of Circe's breeding (7.280-283). Virgil quietly drops the Odyssean ancestry of the Latin king but keeps Circe in the family background.

sources.cite: Homer, Odyssey 10.210 (Circe's house and enchanted beasts)
Hesiod, Theogony 1011-1013 (Circe bears Agrius and Latinus to Odysseus)
J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 7.170 (on Picus and Circe, 7.189-191)

title: Erato, Muse of love poetry
greek: Nunc age, qui reges, Erato, quae tempora rerum, / quis Latio antiquo fuerit status ...
short: Virgil opens his second half by invoking Erato, the Muse of love poetry, an unexpected choice for a war narrative.
body: This is the poem's second proem, matching 'Musa, mihi causas memora' at 1.8. Erato's name is linked with eros, and she was the Muse of love lyric. Apollonius of Rhodes had invoked her at the start of Argonautica 3, where Medea falls in love with Jason, and Virgil's readers would have heard that echo. The choice fits: the war of Books VII-XII is fought over a marriage, Lavinia's, and Amata, Turnus and Juno all act out of passion about that bride. Servius, by contrast, takes a relaxed view: the poet invokes Erato, or Calliope, or any Muse at all. Note the Roman, annalistic language: 'kings', 'times', 'the state of ancient Latium'. Compare the later appeals to the Muses at 7.641 and to Calliope at 9.525.

sources.cite: Servius, Commentary on the Aeneid (ed. G. Thilo, Leipzig, 1881), on Aen. 7.37
Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 3.1-5 (invocation of Erato)
Virgil, Aeneid 7.37, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)

title: 'A greater work': the Iliadic Aeneid
greek: maior rerum mihi nascitur ordo, / maius opus moveo
short: Virgil announces that the second half of the poem, the war in Italy, is the greater theme.
body: Readers have long divided the Aeneid into an 'Odyssean' half (Books I-VI, wanderings) and an 'Iliadic' half (Books VII-XII, war). Here the poet signals the turn himself: 'A greater history opens before me, a greater work I essay' (maior rerum ordo, maius opus). It is a surprising claim after the fall of Troy and the descent to the underworld, and it reflects the Roman view that wars and the founding of states are epic's highest subject ('grim wars ... kings whom honour drove on death'). The Iliadic model appears at once: a Trojan 'Achilles' is foretold to be waiting in Latium (6.89, 'alius Latio iam partus Achilles'), there is a fight over a woman, and a great catalogue of warriors closes the book. Yet the Trojans now play the role of the Greek invaders, which makes the war morally harder to read than Homer's.

sources.cite: Virgil, Aeneid 7.44, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)

title: Latinus and his divine ancestry
greek: Rex arva Latinus et urbes / iam senior longa placidas in pace regebat. / hunc Fauno et nympha genitum Laurente Marica / accipimus; Fauno Picus pater ...
short: Latinus, the aged king of Latium, descends from Saturn through Picus and Faunus: three generations of native Italian gods.
body: Virgil gives Latinus a purely Italian genealogy: Saturn, then Picus (the woodpecker-king), then Faunus (the rustic prophetic god, the Roman Pan), then Latinus himself, born to the nymph Marica of Laurentum. Marica was a goddess worshipped at Minturnae near the mouth of the Liris, as Servius notes. This contrasts with Hesiod's version, where Latinus is a son of Odysseus and Circe. Latinus rules 'in long peace', so the Trojans arrive in a golden-age kingdom that their coming will plunge into war. He has no surviving son, only a daughter of marriageable age, which sets the plot in motion: whoever marries Lavinia inherits the realm. Latinus is a decent but weak king who will finally abdicate his authority (7.600, 'dropped the reins of state').

sources.cite: Servius, Commentary on the Aeneid (ed. G. Thilo, Leipzig, 1881), on Aen. 7.47 (Faunus and Marica)
Virgil, Aeneid 7.45, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
Hesiod, Theogony 1011-1013

title: The laurel and the swarm of bees
greek: laurus erat tecti medio in penetralibus altis ... / Laurentisque ab ea nomen posuisse colonis
short: A swarm of bees settles on Latinus' sacred laurel, and the seer reads it as a foreign army coming to rule the citadel.
body: Two names are explained at once: the people of Laurentum, the 'Laurentines', are said to be named after this laurel (laurus), which Latinus dedicated to Phoebus Apollo. Servius records that the laurel stood in the innermost part of the palace and links the name to the city of Laurolavinium. A swarm of bees settling suddenly was a standard Roman prodigy, and Livy records such swarms among portents. The seer's reading turns on the bees' flight: they come 'from the same quarter' and settle 'on the same quarter', that is, an army will arrive by sea and take the citadel. Bees in Virgil are an image for an ordered community (Georgics 4; the Carthaginians as bees at 1.430-436), so the image also suggests a colony.

anchor: catch fire in her long tresses
title: The omen of Lavinia's burning hair
greek: visa (nefas) longis comprendere crinibus ignem ... / ipsam fore inlustrem fama fatisque canebant, / sed populo magnum portendere bellum
short: Lavinia's hair seems to catch fire without harming her: the omen promises her glory and her people a great war.
body: Lavinia, Latinus' only child, has hardly any lines in the poem; she is defined by what others want of her. This prodigy mirrors the flame that played harmlessly round Ascanius' head in Troy (2.680-691), which Anchises took as a sign to leave. Fire round the head was read as a sign of future greatness in Roman tradition (the story of Servius Tullius, Livy 1.39). The reading is double: fame and destiny for her, a great war for her people. Virgil will return to Lavinia's face 'on fire' with a blush at 12.64-69, a famous and much-debated moment. Mackail's 'oh, horror!' renders the parenthesis nefas, 'a thing unspeakable'.

sources.cite: Virgil, Aeneid 7.71, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 1.39 (flame round the head of the boy Servius Tullius)
Virgil, Aeneid 2.680 (Ascanius' flame), Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)

title: Albunea and the oracle of Faunus
greek: lucosque sub alta / consulit Albunea, nemorum quae maxima sacro / fonte sonat saevamque exhalat opaca mephitim
short: Latinus consults his father Faunus at the sulphurous spring of Albunea, sleeping on the fleeces of sacrificed sheep to receive a dream oracle.
body: Albunea was a sulphurous spring and grove. Horace places the 'echoing house of Albunea' at Tibur (Odes 1.7.12), but Virgil's setting seems to lie near Laurentum, perhaps at the sulphur springs south of Rome; the exact site has been disputed since antiquity. The method described is incubation: the priest sacrifices, lies down at night on the skins of the victims, and receives visions and voices in sleep. The Greeks practised the same at oracles such as that of Amphiaraus at Oropus, where enquirers slept on the fleece of a sacrificed ram (Pausanias 1.34.5). Faunus' answer, delivered from the grove, forbids a Latin marriage: 'foreigners shall come to be thy sons'. 'Mephitis' (mephitim) is the deadly vapour itself, also a goddess of such exhalations (compare Amsanctus, 7.563-571).

sources.cite: Virgil, Aeneid 7.81, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
Horace, Odes 1.7.12 ('domus Albuneae resonantis')
C. T. Lewis and C. Short, A Latin Dictionary (Oxford, 1879), s.v. mephitis
Pausanias, Description of Greece 1.34.5 (sleeping on a ram's fleece at the oracle of Amphiaraus)

title: The prophecy of the eaten tables fulfilled
greek: 'Heus! etiam mensas consumimus?' inquit Iulus
short: When the hungry Trojans eat the flat bread they used as plates, Iulus' joke fulfils the old prophecy that they would 'eat their tables' where they were to settle.
body: The Harpy Celaeno had threatened in Book III that the Trojans would not wall their city until hunger forced them to gnaw their tables (3.255-257); Helenus later told them not to fear it (3.394-395). The prophecy turns out to be harmless: the 'tables' are wheaten cakes used as platters. Aeneas seizes the boy's words as an omen (Roman belief held that a chance utterance could be a divine sign, an omen to be 'caught'), and greets the land: 'here is home; this is our native country'. Conington notes the inconsistency: Aeneas now attributes the prophecy to Anchises, not Celaeno, and he counts it among the discrepancies between Book III and the rest of the poem that Virgil's death left unrevised.

Virgil, Aeneid 3.255 (Celaeno's prophecy), Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
Virgil, Aeneid 7.116, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)

title: Picus, the lituus and the ancile
greek: ipse Quirinali lituo parvaque sedebat / succinctus trabea laevaque ancile gerebat / Picus
short: The statue of Picus in Latinus' palace carries the augur's curved staff, the striped royal robe and the sacred shield: emblems of later Roman religion.
body: Latinus' palace is half temple, half senate-house, and Virgil fills it with Roman antiquities: the inaugural sceptre, the fasces, banquets after sacrifice, statues of ancestors, and spoils on the doors. Picus wears the trabea (a short robe with purple stripes, worn by kings and augurs) and holds the lituus, the curved staff with which an augur marked out the sky; it is called 'Quirinal' because Romulus (Quirinus) was the first augur. The ancile is the figure-of-eight shield of the Salii, Mars' leaping priests. Picus is also a bird, the woodpecker (picus Martius), important in augury; Virgil alludes to the tale, told at length by Ovid (Met. 14.320-396), that Circe turned him into one when he refused her love. Conington calls Virgil 'a lover of antiquity' rather than a strict antiquarian.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 7.187 (Quirinali lituo, trabea, ancile)

title: 'Saturn's people': Italy's golden-age justice
greek: Saturni gentem haud vinclo nec legibus aequam, / sponte sua veterisque dei se more tenentem
short: Latinus describes his Latins as Saturn's people, just by their own free will and not by laws: an idealised golden-age Italy.
body: Saturn, driven from heaven by Jupiter, was believed to have hidden in Latium and ruled there in a golden age (told fully by Evander at 8.319-327). Latinus' boast that his people are righteous because, in Mackail's words, 'no laws fetter' them 'to justice' recalls the golden age of Hesiod and of Ovid (Met. 1.89-93), when people kept faith without punishment. The irony is sharp: within a few hundred lines this same people, maddened by Allecto, will rush into war. Some readers see Virgil questioning whether such innocence can survive history; others note that Book VIII offers a less flattering picture of the first Italians ('a tribe of men born of stocks and hard oak'). Compare Anchises' prophecy that Augustus will refound the golden age in Latium (6.792-794).

sources.cite: Virgil, Aeneid 7.202, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 8.319 (Saturn in Latium)
Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.89-93 (the golden age without laws)

title: Corythus and Dardanus' Italian origin
greek: hinc illum Corythi Tyrrhena ab sede profectum
short: Latinus recalls that Dardanus, ancestor of the Trojans, was born in Italy at Etruscan Corythus, so Aeneas' coming is really a homecoming.
body: This is one of Virgil's boldest adjustments of myth. In Greek tradition Dardanus came from Arcadia or Samothrace; Virgil makes him an Italian from Corythus, a town in Etruria (later identified with Cortona). The idea was first announced by the Penates in Aeneas' dream at 3.163-171 ('hence Dardanus sprang') and is repeated by Ilioneus here ('hinc Dardanus ortus', 7.240). It turns the Trojan settlement from a conquest into a return: Apollo's command to 'seek out your ancient mother' (3.96) was really a call to Italy. Latinus says Dardanus passed by Samothrace on his way to Phrygia and is now a god among the stars. Corythus appears again at 9.10, where Iris tells Turnus that Aeneas has gone to its 'utmost cities' to raise the Etruscans.

sources.cite: Virgil, Aeneid 7.205, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
Virgil, Aeneid 3.163 (the Penates reveal Dardanus' Italian origin), Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
C. T. Lewis and C. Short, A Latin Dictionary (Oxford, 1879), s.v. Corythus

title: 'Flectere si nequeo superos, Acheronta movebo'
greek: flectere si nequeo superos, Acheronta movebo
short: Juno, unable to stop Aeneas, vows to raise hell instead: 'if I cannot bend the gods above, I will move Acheron.'
body: Juno's second great monologue answers her first (1.37-49). Seeing the Trojans settling happily, she admits she cannot prevent fate, Lavinia's marriage or Aeneas' kingdom, but she can delay it and make it cost blood. Conington notes the near-pun on movebo, 'move' both as persuading and as setting powers in motion, set against flectere, 'bend'. Acheron, a river of the underworld, stands for the infernal powers, and she will in fact summon the Fury Allecto from below. The line became one of the most quoted in Latin: Freud used it as the epigraph of The Interpretation of Dreams (1900), reading it as the repressed unconscious forcing its way up. Note Juno's claim to wrong like Mars against the Lapiths and Diana against Calydon (7.304-307): she seeks divine precedent for punishing the innocent.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 7.312 (movebo)
Virgil, Aeneid 7.312, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
Virgil, Aeneid 1.37 (Juno's first monologue), Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)

title: Bellona as pronuba; Hecuba's firebrand
greek: sanguine Troiano et Rutulo dotabere, virgo, / et Bellona manet te pronuba. nec face tantum / Cisseis praegnas ignis enixa iugalis
short: Juno turns the wedding into war: Lavinia's dowry will be Trojan and Rutulian blood, and Bellona, goddess of war, will be her matron of honour.
body: The pronuba was the married woman who led a Roman bride to the marriage-bed; Juno herself is the goddess of marriage, and at 4.166 she acted as pronuba at Dido's 'wedding' in the cave. Here she hands the role to Bellona, the Roman war-goddess. 'Cisseus' daughter' is Hecuba (Virgil follows Euripides in making Cisseus her father, where Homer names Dymas), who dreamed when pregnant with Paris that she bore a firebrand that burned Troy. Juno predicts that Venus has borne 'a second Paris', Aeneas, whose marriage will again set a city ablaze. Conington notes the double sense of taedae and ignis iugalis: the wedding torch and the fire of war. Turnus will develop the same Paris-Helen analogy against Aeneas (9.136-142).

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 7.320 (ignis iugalis, Cisseis)
Virgil, Aeneid 4.166 (Juno as pronuba at Dido's union), Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
C. T. Lewis and C. Short, A Latin Dictionary (Oxford, 1879), s.v. pronuba

title: Allecto the Fury
greek: luctificam Allecto dirarum ab sede dearum / infernisque ciet tenebris
short: Juno summons Allecto, one of the three Furies, whose name means 'unceasing' and whose delight is in war, anger and family strife.
body: The Furies (Greek Erinyes, Latin Dirae or Furiae) were avengers of crimes, especially within families; their usual names are Allecto, Megaera and Tisiphone. Allecto's Greek name, Alekto, means 'the unresting'. Juno calls her 'virgin born of Night' (7.331), following Aeschylus, who makes the Erinyes daughters of Night in the Eumenides. Virgil uses her as the agent of madness (furor) who sets brothers against brothers and 'overturns families with hatreds': the war she starts will feel like a civil war among peoples destined to be one. Conington notes the dirae deae and explains her 'thousand names' (7.337) by the many titles of gods. She works on three targets in turn: Amata (the mother), Turnus (the suitor) and the country people through Ascanius' hunt. Scholars have also seen behind her the Discordia of Ennius' Annales, which opened the gates of war.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 7.324 (luctificam, dirae deae; and on 7.337, mille nomina)
Aeschylus, Eumenides 416 (the Erinyes as daughters of Night)
C. T. Lewis and C. Short, A Latin Dictionary (Oxford, 1879), s.v. Alecto (Allecto)

title: Amata and the serpent
greek: huic dea caeruleis unum de crinibus anguem / conicit, inque sinum praecordia ad intima subdit
short: Allecto slips a snake from her hair into Queen Amata's breast; it becomes her necklace and hair-ribbon and fills her with madness against the Trojan marriage.
body: Amata ('beloved') is Latinus' queen and Turnus' champion; she is already angry before Allecto arrives, and the Fury's poison only inflames what is there. The serpent works invisibly, becoming her twisted gold necklace and the ribbon of her headband: madness disguised as the ornaments of a queen. Her first speech is still reasoned. She casts Aeneas as Paris, the Phrygian shepherd who carried Helen off (7.363-364), and argues that Turnus himself counts as a 'foreigner' by descent from Inachus and Acrisius of Argos (7.371-372). Virgil shows the infection advancing in stages, then the outburst. Amata's story ends with her suicide when she believes Turnus dead (12.593-603).

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 7.323 (summary of 341-372: the snake planted in the queen's bosom)
Virgil, Aeneid 7.341, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
Virgil, Aeneid 12.593 (Amata's death), Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)

title: The simile of the whipped top
greek: ceu quondam torto volitans sub verbere turbo, / quem pueri magno in gyro vacua atria circum / intenti ludo exercent
short: Amata rushing madly through the city is compared to a spinning top whipped round an empty hall by absorbed children.
body: This domestic simile is startling in epic. A turbo was a top driven by lashing it with a whip; boys watch it 'wondering' as the blows 'give it life'. The point is not only speed but helplessness: Amata is driven by blows from outside, just as she is driven by Allecto, and the children's innocent game contrasts with the horror. Conington notes that the turbo was the Greek rhombos or bembix and cites a parallel in Tibullus (1.5.3-4); he observes that the 'empty halls' (atria) suggest the great houses of patrician families, giving the toy some dignity. The image of a woman driven by a goddess like an object under the lash recalls Dido 'like a stricken deer' (4.68-73).

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 7.378 (turbo; Callimachus and Tibullus parallels)
C. T. Lewis and C. Short, A Latin Dictionary (Oxford, 1879), s.v. turbo
Virgil, Aeneid 7.378, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)

title: Amata's feigned Bacchic rites
greek: simulato numine Bacchi ... 'euhoe Bacche' fremens
short: Amata pretends to be possessed by Bacchus and hides Lavinia in the mountains, leading the Latin matrons out in wild Bacchic worship.
body: The scene uses the full apparatus of the cult of Dionysus (Bacchus): the cry euhoe, fawnskins, the thyrsus (a vine-wreathed wand, here 'spears of vine'), hair loosed to the winds, dancing on the mountains and torches. Conington calls the description 'altogether Greek' and thinks of Euripides' Bacchae, where Theban women likewise abandon their homes. But Roman readers would also think of the Bacchanalia that the Senate violently suppressed in 186 BC (Livy 39.8-19) as a danger to order and families. Amata's madness begins as pretence (simulato) and becomes real. Her torch is a grim joke: it is the wedding torch, as she 'chants the wedding of Turnus and her daughter'. Women breaking out of the household is, in this poem, a sign that the social order is collapsing.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 7.385 (simulato numine; Euripides' Bacchae; the Bacchanalia)
Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 39.8-19 (suppression of the Bacchanalia, 186 BC)
C. T. Lewis and C. Short, A Latin Dictionary (Oxford, 1879), s.v. thyrsus

title: Ardea, Turnus' city
greek: locus Ardea quondam / dictus avis, et nunc magnum manet Ardea nomen, / sed fortuna fuit
short: Ardea, the Rutulian city of Turnus, was founded, Virgil says, by Danae of Argos; 'Ardea' once meant 'heron', and only the great name now remains.
body: Ardea lay about 35 km south of Rome near the coast and was once a powerful Rutulian town. Virgil gives it a Greek founder, Danae, mother of Perseus, who drifted to Italy with Argive settlers (the 'people of Acrisius', her father). This makes Turnus partly Argive, which Amata stresses (7.371-372) and his shield's Io and Inachus advertise (7.789-792). 'Ardea' is also the Latin for heron; Ovid tells how a heron rose from the ashes of the city when Aeneas' men burned it (Met. 14.573-580). The phrase 'sed fortuna fuit' (Mackail: 'its fortune is no more') is one of Virgil's laments for faded Italian towns, written when Ardea was a small place.

sources.cite: Virgil, Aeneid 7.406, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
Ovid, Metamorphoses 14.573-580 (the heron rises from burnt Ardea)
C. T. Lewis and C. Short, A Latin Dictionary (Oxford, 1879), s.v. ardea

title: Allecto's torch and the boiling cauldron
greek: magno veluti cum flamma sonore / virgea suggeritur costis undantis aeni
short: Allecto appears to Turnus as the old priestess Calybe; mocked, she reveals herself, hurls a torch at him, and his rage boils like water in a cauldron over a fire.
body: The scene has three movements. Disguised as Calybe, priestess of Juno, Allecto urges Turnus to war. Turnus scornfully tells the 'old woman' to keep to her temple, since war belongs to men: a confident, even reasonable answer. Allecto then reveals herself in Fury form and drives her torch into his breast. The simile of water boiling over in a bronze cauldron as twigs are piled under it is Homeric: in Iliad 21.362-365 the river Xanthus seethes like a cauldron under Hephaestus' fire. It pictures Turnus' anger (ira) as something fed from outside until it overflows. Scholars disagree on how far Turnus is responsible for what follows: Virgil gives him real grievances, but also shows a temperament the Fury's fire catches easily.

sources.cite: Homer, Iliad 21.362 (Xanthus boils like a cauldron)
Virgil, Aeneid 7.462, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 7.445

title: Silvia's stag: the cause of the war
greek: cervus erat forma praestanti et cornibus ingens ... / Silvia ... adsuetum imperiis soror omni Silvia cura / mollibus intexens ornabat cornua sertis
short: Allecto sets Ascanius' hounds on a tame stag loved by Silvia, daughter of the royal herdsman Tyrrheus; his wounding brings the country people out to fight.
body: The war's immediate cause is pathetically small: a pet stag, garlanded and washed by a girl, shot by a boy eager for glory ('kindled with desire of the chief honour', laudis amore). Virgil presents it as a pastoral world broken into by epic violence. The stag 'filling all the house with moans as of one beseeching' recalls the wounded deer of the Dido simile (4.68-73). Conington suggests that the name Silvia ('of the woods') links her with early Latin legend: Rea Silvia, mother of Romulus, and Silvius, Aeneas' son (6.763). Tyrrheus, master of the royal herds, is a herdsman, not a king. The ancients debated the 'just cause' of wars; Virgil makes this one accidental, divinely engineered, and yet still a matter of human anger.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 7.475 (notes on Silvia and Tyrrheus)
Virgil, Aeneid 7.483, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)

title: Allecto's horn: Trivia's lake, Nar and Velinus
greek: audiit et Triviae longe lacus, audiit amnis / sulpurea Nar albus aqua fontesque Velini
short: Allecto's war-horn echoes across Italy, heard at Diana's lake at Nemi, the sulphurous river Nar and the springs of Velinus.
body: Trivia ('of the three ways') is a title of Diana-Hecate, worshipped where roads meet. 'Trivia's lake' is the Lake of Nemi in the Alban Hills, beside the grove of Diana of Aricia (see Virbius, 7.761-782). The Nar (modern Nera) is whitened by sulphur; the Velinus (Velino) flows from the Sabine hills and joins the Nar at the waterfall of Marmore. The list sweeps from the Alban Hills to Umbria: the sound travels far beyond any real hearing distance, showing that the whole of Italy is being summoned. The 'pastoral war-note' (pastorale signum) on a curved herdsman's horn is a rustic version of the military trumpet. Mothers clutching their children (7.518) give the scene its human cost.

sources.cite: C. T. Lewis and C. Short, A Latin Dictionary (Oxford, 1879), s.v. trivius (Trivia)
Virgil, Aeneid 7.511, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
Virgil, Aeneid 7.516 (Triviae lacus, Nar, Velinus), Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)

title: The Vale of Amsanctus
greek: est locus Italiae medio sub montibus altis, / nobilis et fama multis memoratus in oris, / Amsancti valles
short: Allecto returns to the underworld through Amsanctus, a valley of deadly volcanic gases in the land of the Hirpini, thought to be a breathing-hole of hell.
body: The Valle d'Ansanto in the southern Apennines, near modern Rocca San Felice, still gives off lethal carbon dioxide and sulphurous gas from a bubbling pool. The Romans worshipped the goddess Mefitis there; Pliny the Elder notes a place 'at the temple of Mefitis' among the Hirpini where those who enter die (Natural History 2.208). Virgil makes it the exit for the Fury, a 'breathing-hole of the grim lord of hell' and a chasm into Acheron, in the very middle of Italy. The detail roots the supernatural in real landscape, as with the sulphur at Albunea (7.84), and suggests that the hell Juno has stirred (7.312) lies close beneath Italian soil.

title: The Gates of War (Janus' temple) and the Gabine cincture
greek: sunt geminae Belli portae ... / ... Quirinali trabea cinctuque Gabino / insignis reserat stridentia limina consul
short: Virgil describes the Roman ritual of opening the 'Gates of War' (the temple of Janus); when Latinus refuses, Juno herself bursts them open.
body: At Rome the shrine of Janus Geminus in the Forum had two doors that stood open in war and closed in peace; Livy says Numa built it as an index of war and peace (1.19). Closing them was rare: Augustus boasted that they were shut three times in his reign (Res Gestae 13). Jupiter had promised that under Augustus 'the dread Gates of War shall be closed', with Furor chained inside (1.293-296); here the gates open in primitive Latium. The consul wears the trabea and the cinctus Gabinus, an archaic way of girding the toga with one end wrapped round the body. Conington reports Servius' story that the people of Gabii, attacked during a sacrifice, fought in this dress. Latinus will not touch the gates; Juno, 'Saturnian queen of heaven', thrusts them open herself, in a scene many scholars connect with Ennius' Discordia breaking the gates of war.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 7.607 (Belli portae; and on 7.612, cinctus Gabinus)
Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 1.19 (Numa's temple of Janus)

anchor: Open now the gates of Helicon
title: Invocation and the Catalogue of Italians
greek: Pandite nunc Helicona, deae, cantusque movete
short: Virgil invokes the Muses of Helicon before a long catalogue of the Italian leaders and peoples who join Turnus, modelled on Homer's Catalogue of Ships.
body: Homer prefaces the Catalogue of Ships with an appeal to the Muses, who are present and know everything, while mortals hear only rumour (Iliad 2.484-493). Conington shows that Virgil closely recalls this contrast in 7.645-646 ('you remember, divine ones ... to us but a breath of rumour'). The 'gates of Helicon' (Mount Helicon in Boeotia, home of the Muses) open just after the Gates of War have been opened, a pointed pairing. The catalogue that follows (7.647-817) is a roll-call of early Italy: leaders, towns, rivers, weapons and local customs, including many names that were famous or faded in Virgil's day. It begins with the impious Mezentius and ends with the brilliant Camilla, and gives the Italians real dignity: these are the ancestors of Rome too.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 7.641 (Pandite nunc Helicona; Il. 2.484 ff.)
Homer, Iliad 2.484
Virgil, Aeneid 7.641, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)

title: Mezentius, contemptor divum
greek: Primus init bellum Tyrrhenis asper ab oris / contemptor divum Mezentius
short: Mezentius, the expelled Etruscan tyrant of Caere (Agylla), leads the catalogue and is marked from the start as a 'scorner of the gods'.
body: Mezentius was a figure of early Latin legend: Livy makes him king of Caere and ally of Turnus (1.2). Macrobius preserves an older tradition, going back to Cato, that he demanded for himself the first-fruits owed to the gods, which may explain the epithet contemptor divum. Book VIII tells of his tyranny and his gruesome punishment of binding the living to the dead (8.481-488). His son Lausus is introduced here as beautiful and 'worthy to have had another than Mezentius for father'. Their deaths in Book X are among the most moving in the poem: the impious father finally shows real love and grief for his son. Agylla is the Greek name of Caere (modern Cerveteri).

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 7.647 (summary: Mezentius and Lausus lead the army from Agylla)
Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 1.2 (Mezentius king of Caere)

title: Clausus and the Claudian family
greek: Ecce Sabinorum prisco de sanguine magnum / agmen agens Clausus magnique ipse agminis instar, / Claudia nunc a quo diffunditur et tribus et gens
short: Clausus, a Sabine leader, is made the ancestor of the Claudii, the great Roman family to which Augustus' wife Livia and stepson Tiberius belonged.
body: Roman tradition said the Claudii came to Rome from the Sabine town of Regillum under Attius (Atta) Clausus around 504 BC, becoming Appius Claudius (Livy 2.16). Conington points out that Virgil takes this name back into the heroic age, centuries earlier, so that a noble house of his own day appears among Turnus' allies. The phrase 'a great host himself' (magnique ipse agminis instar) means his courage was worth an army. 'Since Rome was shared with the Sabines' alludes to the union of Romans and Sabines under Romulus and Titus Tatius after the rape of the Sabine women (pictured on the shield, 8.635-641). Such family compliments are typical of the catalogue, which honours Italian and Roman origins on the enemy side.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 7.706 (Clausus and the Claudii)
Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 2.16 (Attius Clausus migrates to Rome)

title: The Allia, river of the 'black day'
greek: quosque secans infaustum interluit Allia nomen
short: The Allia was the stream where the Gauls crushed the Roman army in 390 BC; its anniversary remained a day of ill omen in the Roman calendar.
body: Virgil names a small tributary of the Tiber north of Rome and at once calls it 'an unlucky name', looking forward from the heroic age to Roman history. At the Allia the Gauls under Brennus routed the Romans before sacking Rome (Livy 5.37-38). The date, the dies Alliensis in July, was marked as a day on which no public business should be done (Livy 6.1.11). Conington explains the allusion. Such flashes of later history inside the catalogue remind readers that these peoples' lands will see Roman disasters as well as triumphs; the sack by the Gauls also appears on Aeneas' shield (8.652-662).

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 7.717 (Allia and the dies Alliensis)
Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 5.37-38 (the battle of the Allia)
Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 6.1.11 (the day made nefastus)

title: Virbius, son of Hippolytus
greek: Ibat et Hippolyti proles pulcherrima bello, / Virbius
short: Virbius is the son of Hippolytus, who was brought back to life by Asclepius and hidden by Diana in her grove at Aricia under the new name Virbius.
body: Hippolytus, the chaste son of Theseus, was falsely accused by his stepmother Phaedra and killed when his horses bolted at a bull from the sea (Euripides' Hippolytus). Diana, whom he served, had him revived by Asclepius ('the Phoebus-born', son of Apollo, with 'Paean's herbs'); Jupiter struck the healer dead with a thunderbolt for raising a mortal. Diana then hid Hippolytus at Aricia as Virbius, a name ancient writers explained as vir bis, 'twice a man'. Horses were banned from her grove at Nemi because of his death. Conington notes Servius' objection that the celibate Hippolytus should have no son, and suggests Virgil keeps father and son distinct. The cult at Nemi later inspired J. G. Frazer's The Golden Bough (1890). Ovid tells the story twice (Met. 15.497-546; Fasti 6.737-762).

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 7.761 (Virbius, Aricia, Egeria, Paeoniis herbis)
Ovid, Metamorphoses 15.497-546 (Hippolytus becomes Virbius)
C. T. Lewis and C. Short, A Latin Dictionary (Oxford, 1879), s.v. Virbius

title: Turnus' Chimaera helmet and Io shield
greek: cui triplici crinita iuba galea alta Chimaeram / sustinet ... at levem clipeum sublatis cornibus Io / auro insignibat
short: Turnus' helmet bears the fire-breathing Chimaera, which rages more as the battle grows; his shield shows Io turned into a heifer, guarded by Argus.
body: The Chimaera, the lion-goat-serpent slain by Bellerophon, breathes 'Aetnean fires' on Turnus' crest and grows fiercer as the fighting does: an emblem of his own rising fury. The shield shows Io, daughter of the river-god Inachus, whom Jupiter loved and Juno turned into a heifer and set the hundred-eyed Argus to guard (told in Ovid, Met. 1.583-750). The image advertises Turnus' Argive descent through Inachus (7.371-372), but it is double-edged: Io was a victim of Juno's anger, the same goddess who now drives Turnus. Many readers set this shield against Aeneas' shield in Book VIII: Turnus carries a myth of the past, Aeneas the history of Rome's future.

sources.cite: C. T. Lewis and C. Short, A Latin Dictionary (Oxford, 1879), s.v. Chimaera
Virgil, Aeneid 7.789 (the Io shield), Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.583-750 (Io, Argus and Inachus)

title: Camilla, the warrior maiden
greek: hos super advenit Volsca de gente Camilla ... / illa vel intactae segetis per summa volaret / gramina nec teneras cursu laesisset aristas
short: Camilla, a Volscian warrior-maiden who has never touched the distaff, closes the catalogue; she could run over standing corn without bruising the ears.
body: Camilla is Virgil's own creation, a Latin Amazon (compare Penthesilea at 1.490-493). She rejects 'Minerva's distaff', the work that defined Roman women, for war. The hyperbole of running over corn and waves without wetting her feet recalls the mares of Erichthonius in Iliad 20.226-229, which ran over corn and sea without breaking the ears. The crowd's wonder at her purple, golden hair-clasp, Lycian quiver and shepherd's myrtle spear mixes royalty with pastoral simplicity. Placing her last gives the catalogue a dazzling finale. Her story is told fully in Book XI, where Diana explains her wild upbringing and she dies after a heroic aristeia (11.532-835).

sources.cite: Homer, Iliad 20.226 (Erichthonius' mares run over corn)
Virgil, Aeneid 7.803, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
Virgil, Aeneid 11.532 (Diana's account of Camilla), Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
